extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century public / readers of The Spectator; genteel readers interested in manners, theatre, and social criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Short, didactic essays (The Spectator) offering standards and judgments about social behaviour, taste in theatre/acting, and the moral use of wit and satire. The pieces mix moral guidance, practical remedies for social ills, and aesthetic criteria for theatrical representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and effects of envy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Envious Man is in pain upon occasions which should give pleasure; all perfections of fellow-creatures are odious to him; he cannot rejoice in another's merit or success and lives as if all mankind are plotting against his quiet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observes signs of envy (resentment at youth, beauty, valour, wisdom), notes its misery and apostasy from approving what is good; examples include those who seek to disparage or divide credit for nameless merit. Anti-pattern: attempting to suppress an author's reputation or redistribute praise to diminish a single person's fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: How public figures can avoid provoking envy
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid the envy that may accrue from public success, the writer recommends occasional self-deprecations and revealing small imperfections (e.g., describing one's face) so as to 'resign pretensions to beauty' as reputation grows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical remedy: moderate displays of accomplishment, admit faults or dullness from time to time to console envious readers. Example: the Spectator promises to be sometimes dull and to disclose his person to soften envy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impudence (the 'Starer') as a social offence
rubrics_metrics.description: Impudence committed by the eyes — 'Starers' who stare impertinently in public, especially in sacred places like churches — is a serious aggravation of bad behaviour because it violates the sanctity of the place and disturbs others' devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies: direct confrontation by a male friend to 'encounter the Eyes' of the Starer; practical tactics (placing an opponent opposite to meet his eyes). Notes that Starers are not usually amendable to reason; social censure and active defence of the modest are advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: No excuse by claiming 'humour' for deliberate impudence
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who knowingly professes impudence and then cloaks it as 'humour' is more culpable than the merely impudent; consciousness of the fault removes any mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative stance: intentional impudence demands shame; awareness of being impudent makes one inexcusable. Advice: genuine modesty (blushing) is expected; claiming humour is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural varieties of impudence (observational criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impudence manifests differently by nation: English impudence is sullen and insolent, Scotch untractable and rapacious, Irish absurd and fawning; the Irish impudence can be comic and sometimes succeeds where English coxcombry fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an explanatory observation about social manners and their different effects on the public; not prescriptive but aids in diagnosing behaviour and its reception by women and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of good theatrical representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A good play or opera should concern human life and be a picture of nature; entertainments that rely on improbability, incoherence, or spectacle that dismisses understanding produce the 'laughter of fools' and 'wonder of idiots.' Scenes (e.g., madness) should represent disturbance of a noble mind, not mere appetite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of current stage practice: actors and managers ought to aim for fidelity to human nature and humane passion. Anti-patterns: incoherent plots, monstrous improbabilities, caricatured madness (e.g., madness represented as mere thirst or appetite), and devices that show motionless 'ornaments' rather than human action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting should express sense and humane passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful acting requires understanding of the passions; true madness on stage should be shown as the disturbance of a noble mind (akin to grief), not as crude appetite or mere physical antics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from correspondence: actors reduced to pantomime (pump, chair, flower-pot) or performing without sense are condemned. Advice to players: study and represent the underlying humane motives and passions rather than mechanical gestures or nonsensical props.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper moral use of wit and ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Lampoons and satyrs written with wit but ill-nature are like poison'd darts: witty ridicule that targets private persons, raises uneasiness, or exposes families to derision is barbarous and inhuman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative boundary: wit should not be used maliciously to wound reputation; satire ought not to be the instrument of private malice. Anti-pattern: anonymity used to inflict private injury under cover of humour; vicious persons who combine wit with vice are singled out as socially dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice on choice of profession for livelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents and young men should consider genius and abilities when choosing professions; professions like divinity, law, and physic are overstocked while trade (commerce) flourishes by multitudes and offers honest industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socio-economic recommendation: avoid forcing children into crowded learned professions where even merit may perish; a trading nation offers many opportunities where industry and frugality can lead to success. Example: a sober frugal person might thrive in trade though starve in physic.
